summary: For ages 7-8, solve number and practical problems using three-digit place value to 1000, applying it flexibly rather than first learning it. The central objective is flexible re-unitising: seeing that the SAME number can be decomposed many equivalent ways (340 = 3 hundreds 4 tens = 34 tens = 300 + 40) and choosing the view that fits the problem. Children work 'how many tens/hundreds' questions, missing-digit clues (4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones give 407), and money/measure contexts, explaining and checking their reasoning.
misconceptions: Only seeing canonical partition (340 = 300 + 40) and missing '34 tens'.
Counting in ones instead of using place-value structure.
Mishandling internal zeros in problem numbers (407).
Not mapping money/measure contexts onto place-value columns.

activities.title: Place-value problem workbench: re-unitise to answer
steps: Read a problem card such as 'How many tens are in 340?'
Build 340 with place-value pieces (three hundred-flats, four tens-rods) or arrow cards.
Exchange each hundred-flat for ten tens-rods on an exchange pad and watch 340 reassemble as 34 tens-rods, then read off the answer: 34 tens.
Repeat for another number (e.g. how many tens in 350? how many hundreds in 680?) and say which decomposition you used.
Name the strategy you used each time ('I re-unitised the hundreds into tens').
activities.insight: The same number can be re-unitised into equivalent decompositions; you pick the view that answers the question, and you can check by rebuilding the original number.

activities.title: Money and measures as place-value columns
steps: Solve a money problem such as '£4.07 = how many pence?' using a money tray (pounds, 10p, 1p).
Counting the amount in pence, map pounds onto hundreds (£1 = 100p), 10p onto tens, and 1p onto ones, lining them up in place-value columns.
Work a small shopping total using the same columns you used for whole numbers.
State how the money columns mirror hundreds/tens/ones.
activities.insight: Money (pounds / 10p / 1p) mirrors the hundreds/tens/ones structure, so a shopping total is solved with the identical place-value reasoning.

activities.title: Missing-digit and missing-value clues
steps: Read a clue such as 'I have 4 hundreds, 0 tens and 7 ones — what number am I?' and build the number (407).
Honour the placeholder: put no tens pieces in the tens column but keep the column, and write a 0 digit there when recording, so the number is written correctly as 407, not 47.
Work an inverse/missing-value problem, e.g. '__ tens make 340' or 'a number has 34 tens and no ones — what is it?'
Explain how you knew where each digit belonged.
activities.insight: Place value is a two-way tool: you can reason backwards from a description to the number, and internal zeros act as placeholders that must be honoured.

activities.title: Talk-it-through: how did you decide?
steps: Respond to a riddle or problem and explain, step by step, how you worked it out.

Answer probes such as: 'How many tens are in 350? Is there more than one way to see that?', 'Could 350 also be 35 tens — how would you check?', 'What did you already know about how numbers are built that helped you decide?'
Test whether the same thinking helps for 'how many tens are in 352' and say what changes.
Justify your chosen decomposition and check it by rebuilding the number.
activities.insight: Being able to articulate why a chosen decomposition fits — and to check it — shows place value is held as a flexible strategy, not a single fixed label.

activities.title: Consolidation problems and worked reference
steps: Answer a mix of items: 'how many tens in 340?', '£4.07 = __ pence', 'which number has 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones?', and match each problem to its useful partition.
Attempt a multi-step word problem in a real context (e.g. money).
Use a worked example of a how-many-tens problem as a reference: step through the reasoning when stuck, rather than copying the answer.
activities.insight: Varied practice consolidates flexible partitioning and lets the child recognise which decomposition a given problem rewards.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Someone tells you 350 is made of 3 hundreds and 5 tens. Is that the only way to see what 350 is made of, or are there others? If you got a problem like “how many tens are in 350?”, how would you decide what the number is really made of? Talk me through it.' Surface the thinking — don't grade it.
checkAnswer: Not scored. A rich response recognises 350 can be viewed in several equivalent ways (3 hundreds 5 tens, OR 35 tens, OR 350 ones) and that you choose the view that fits the problem — and can check by rebuilding the number.
